faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a system of two stars orbiting each other in such a way that they periodically pass in front of each other as seen from Earth. Each time one star blocks the light of the other, the total brightness of the system dips. By observing these brightness dips over time, astronomers can learn about the stars' sizes, temperatures, and orbital properties.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary star?

faqs.answer: A candidate is a star whose light curve shows a pattern consistent with an eclipsing binary. A confirmed candidate is one that has passed Star Vetter's automated pixel-level check, which verifies that the brightness dips originate from the target star itself and not from a nearby star whose light accidentally mixed in with the signal. Confirmation here means the candidate survived our pipeline - it does not imply scientific verification or publication.
faqs.question: What's the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' candidate on this site?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter trains machine learning models on thousands of labeled examples to learn which eclipsing binary signals are most reliable. The current model provides a second opinion on candidate quality and outperforms our rule-based baseline. However, this score is not used to gate or filter which candidates get checked - all novel candidates proceed to the pixel-level check regardless of the ML score. The model is a tool for understanding our results, not a decision-maker in the pipeline.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning screening score?

faqs.answer: After a candidate passes statistical tests and novelty screening, it undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This process examines the spatial distribution of the brightness signal across the detector to ensure it is centered on the target star and not caused by a nearby contaminant or instrumental artifact. The check is fully automated and runs the same way for every candidate.
faqs.question: How is each candidate checked?

faqs.answer: Aliasing occurs when the true period is ambiguous from the data. Star Vetter performs an odd/even eclipse-depth test: it compares the brightness dips of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If these depths differ significantly, it suggests the period may be aliased. Such candidates are flagged on their individual pages, and users can inspect the light curve and perform their own follow-up observations to resolve the ambiguity.
faqs.question: What if the eclipse period looks aliased?

faqs.answer: Yes. Every confirmed candidate on this site includes a light curve plot, orbital period, eclipse depths, and relevant metadata. You can download the underlying TESS data and perform your own analysis. Many candidates are bright enough for amateur telescopes or citizen-science programs to observe and help refine the measurements.
faqs.question: Can I verify a confirmed candidate myself?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter's role ends when a candidate is listed on this site. The pipeline does not submit candidates to journals, add them to official catalogs, or coordinate professional follow-up observations. We provide the data and results publicly so that researchers, students, and amateur astronomers can use them for their own purposes. Any further scientific study or confirmation is up to the community.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it's listed here?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically identifies eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. When two stars orbit each other and pass in front of each other from our viewpoint, their combined brightness dips in a telltale pattern. Our pipeline searches the light curves of nearly 18,000 stars observed by TESS, applies statistical tests to separate real signals from noise, checks each candidate against six known variable-star catalogs to flag novel objects, and then runs an automated pixel-level check to confirm the signal comes from the target star itself rather than a nearby contaminant. We've confirmed 260 candidates so far. The vetting process is rigorous: fewer than 10 percent of novel candidates survive the full pipeline, and each confirmed candidate can be inspected in detail on this site. We also train machine learning models on our labeled examples to better understand which signals are trustworthy, continuously improving our methods.
